UPDATE: Build-A-Salad blames permanent closure on diarrhea outbreak linked to lettuce
sources.text:
UPDATE: Local restaurant Build-A-Salad announced that it will permanently close its doors due to the cyclosporiasis outbreak.
Owners of Build-A-Salad, a self-serve salad restaurant located at 129 North Market Street, previously told Local 3 News that they feared this would be the outcome. Business recently dropped from 150-200 customers per day to around 10.
Restaurant owners believe the massive drop in customers is due to the outbreak of cyclosporiasis, an illness that spreads through contaminated food, causing diarrhea, cramping and fatigue.
The Hamilton County Health Department says the illness is most commonly linked to fresh produce, such as leafy greens, herbs and certain fruits.
Build-A-Salad owners state it simply:
“It’s tough being a salad restaurant when everyone is scared of lettuce.”
Read the restaurant’s full Facebook post announcing its closure:
PREVIOUS STORY: It's been a swirl of confusion, with the Federal Drug Administration now saying there is no evidence that all lettuce or iceberg lettuce is contaminated, but many have taken precaution anyway–to the detriment of restaurants.
Sean Alexander is the owner of Northshore's Build-A-Salad, a self-serve restaurant with a singular focus: salads.
He says since the restaurant's opening in February, he’s seen steady business until a few days ago.
“We were doing about 150 to 200 people a day, and as of last Saturday, we dropped down to about 10 a day, so it’s just pretty much cut the business in half,” Alexander says.
He says the sharp drop can be blamed on concerns over the nationwide Cyclospora outbreak, when he noticed customers weren’t showing.
“I didn't really know what had happened, and then people were coming through the doors, and they were saying they had heard about a parasite,” he says.
This has caused many to avoid lettuce and leafy greens altogether, amid uncertainty about which products are affected.
Data gathered by Placer, an analytics platform, says Taco Bell saw foot traffic drop by nearly 20% over three days, while Cava, Chipotle and Panera Bread also saw declines over the same period.
Alexander says his business has even taken steps to address those concerns.
“They heard that it was iceberg lettuce, so we stopped selling iceberg lettuce,” Alexander says.
With the number of customers dwindling, Alexander says he's starting to feel pressure.
“With this going on, it's just a big hit, and we're really not protected against other things like this,” he says. “We've just been trying to do what we can do.”
Despite the restaurant's opening just six months ago, Alexander says he's now having to consider a painstaking decision to close and reinvent.
“I put so much work into this place, and it’s the same thing with our employees–they come to work every day, and they try their hardest,” he says.
He says customers could expect a complete rebrand in the coming weeks, but for now — he's just waiting for concerns to subside.

sources.news_title: What is Cyclospora? Two deaths as US outbreak puts Europe on alert
sources.text:
Cyclospora: Parasite back in the spotlight after two US deaths. Here's what to know about symptoms, transmission, risky foods and the situation in Europe.
Two people have died in Michigan from complications linked to cyclosporiasis, an intestinal infection caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis. They are the first deaths associated with the large outbreak currently affecting the United States, where more than 18,000 cases have been reported since the start of the season, an exceptionally high figure compared with previous years.
Michigan health authorities have said that both victims had serious pre-existing conditions and that dehydration caused by diarrhoea may have worsened their condition. In the state, more than 11,200 cases have been reported, with almost 200 hospital admissions.
What is Cyclospora and how is it transmitted
Cyclosporiasis is caused by a microscopic parasite that can contaminate fresh produce and water. Unlike many intestinal infections, it is not spread directly from person to person: infection almost always occurs through the consumption of contaminated fruit, vegetables or water.
Symptoms include:
- severe, prolonged diarrhoea;
- abdominal cramps;
- nausea;
- loss of appetite;
- fatigue;
- fever in some cases.
Without treatment, the illness can last for several weeks. The main risk is dehydration, which is particularly dangerous for older people, those with weakened immune systems and patients with chronic diseases.
Why cases rise in summer
The increase in infections in the summer months is no coincidence. In the United States, the cyclosporiasis season generally runs from May to August, a period when consumption of fresh produce such as salads, herbs, berries and other raw vegetables increases.
High temperatures and greater circulation of fruit and vegetables also help the parasite spread along the food supply chain. In the US outbreak, investigators are focusing on iceberg lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms, which has already been recalled from the market after being identified as a probable source of contamination.
What about Europe? No major outbreak, but surveillance is being stepped up
At the moment, the European Union is not experiencing a cyclosporiasis epidemic comparable to the one hitting the United States.
According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), cases recorded on the continent are generally sporadic and mostly affect people returning from trips to countries where the parasite is endemic, such as Mexico, Peru, Guatemala and other tropical and subtropical areas. In recent years, only a few outbreaks have been documented in Europe, almost always linked to imported food or infections acquired abroad.
One warning sign comes from the United Kingdom, where between April and mid-July 2026, 67 cases of cyclosporiasis were reported, almost all of them associated with travel to Mexico. For this reason, European health authorities are maintaining heightened surveillance during the summer, when increased international travel and higher consumption of fresh fruit and vegetables can facilitate the importation of new cases.
Why it is being talked about so much right now
The combination of the exceptional outbreak in the United States and the holiday season has put the parasite back in the spotlight. In summer, international travel increases, as does consumption of salads and uncooked foods, along with the chances of exposure to contaminated food and water.
Health authorities therefore recommend a few simple precautions: wash fruit and vegetables thoroughly, drink safe water when travelling, keep food properly refrigerated and see a doctor in the event of persistent diarrhoea, especially if it is accompanied by signs of dehydration or affects vulnerable people.

sources.news_title: Two Deaths Reported as Michigan Cyclospora Outbreak Tops 11,000 Cases
sources.text:
DETROIT ~ Michigan health officials have confirmed the first two deaths connected to the state’s ongoing cyclospora outbreak as the number of reported cases surpassed 11,000, making it one of the largest foodborne illness outbreaks the state has tracked in recent years. State data released Monday showed 11,234 cases and 193 hospitalizations linked to the outbreak.
According to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, both individuals who died had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclospora infection and dehydration. Officials said the illnesses occurred before a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce announced in July and noted that deaths from cyclosporiasis remain uncommon in the United States.
Health investigators continue to examine the source of the outbreak. Federal officials have linked cases in Michigan and several other states to shredded iceberg lettuce served at some Taco Bell restaurants. Taylor Farms subsequently issued a voluntary recall of iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico, and Taco Bell said it is no longer using lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico.
Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes an intestinal illness known as cyclosporiasis. Symptoms can include prolonged diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, fatigue, loss of appetite, and dehydration. While most patients recover, public health experts caution that older adults and people with weakened immune systems or other serious health conditions can face increased risks from complications related to dehydration.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services continues to advise consumers to discard or return recalled iceberg lettuce and to contact a healthcare provider if symptoms develop after consuming potentially contaminated food. The agency said its investigation remains active and case totals could change as additional reports are reviewed.

sources.news_title: Michigan reports first 2 fatalities connected to widespread cyclospora outbreak
sources.text:
State health authorities announced Monday that two Michigan residents have died in connection with an ongoing cyclosporiasis outbreak, marking the first reported fatalities in the nationwide surge of the parasitic illness. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services confirmed that both individuals had “significant underlying health conditions” that may have been complicated by the intestinal infection and severe dehydration. Public health officials declined to release further personal details regarding the deceased patients.
State surveillance data shows Michigan has recorded 11,234 cyclosporiasis cases since tracking commenced on June 22, representing an increase of several hundred cases over recent days. At least 193 patients across the state have required hospitalization due to the severity of their symptoms. Despite the recorded fatalities, medical experts emphasize that fatal outcomes from the microscopic parasite remain exceptionally rare. State health officials noted, “Cyclosporiasis is generally not a life-threatening illness.” They added, “Death resulting from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States.”
Cyclosporiasis stems from consuming food or water contaminated with the microscopic parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis. It infects the small intestine, typically causing severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, fatigue, and weight loss. Because symptoms generally take roughly one to two weeks to manifest following exposure, tracing exact food contamination points poses significant challenges for epidemiologists. The infection is treatable with standard antibiotics prescribed by medical professionals.
Federal agencies, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration, continue investigating multiple clusters across dozens of states. A primary focus of federal inquiries has involved shredded iceberg lettuce produced by Taylor Farms in central Mexico, which led to targeted restaurant supply recalls earlier in the summer. However, health authorities caution that leafy greens, fresh herbs, and imported berries remain potential vectors for the parasite.
To minimize exposure risks, state health representatives recommend thoroughly washing all fresh raw produce under clean running water prior to consumption, though cooking food to 158 degrees Fahrenheit remains the most effective method to eliminate the parasite. Officials advise anyone exhibiting suspicious symptoms to seek prompt medical evaluation. State health representatives emphasized, “Anyone experiencing gastrointestinal illness, such as sudden and ongoing diarrhea, should contact their health care provider and their local health department,” particularly individuals with compromised immune systems or heightened vulnerability to dehydration.

sources.news_title: Two deaths linked to cyclosporiasis in Michigan
sources.text:
Two deaths linked to cyclosporiasis in Michigan
(NYT) — Health officials in Michigan have linked two deaths to cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness caused by the parasite cyclospora. These are the first fatalities associated with a nine-state outbreak connected to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms, a spokesperson for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said.
Both people who died had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” according to an update posted to the Michigan Health Department’s website. Michigan, which is at the center of the nine-state outbreak, has reported 11,234 cases and 193 hospitalizations.
John Guzewich, who worked on food-borne disease outbreaks at the Food and Drug Administration from 1997 to 2011, said he was not aware of any other instances where the CDC had reported deaths in the United States linked to the parasite, which spreads through food or water contaminated with human feces. “This is unprecedented,” he said.
The infection, which causes severe diarrhea that can last from a few days to a month or more, is typically treated with antibiotics. Deaths from cyclosporiasis are atypical in the United States, said Matthew Moore, a food safety microbiologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. But lengthy bouts of diarrhea can be dangerous for vulnerable groups including infants, older adults, and those who are pregnant or have weakened immune systems.
The deaths come during the worst year on record for cyclosporiasis in the United States. Since May 1, the CDC has confirmed or is investigating more than 18,000 cases in 45 states, and has reported 423 hospitalizations.

sources.text:
First two deaths in cyclosporiasis outbreak reported in Michigan as cases surpass 11,000
(ABC) — The first two deaths of the cyclosporiasis outbreak have been reported in Michigan, the state’s health department announced Monday.
Both people had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) added. No additional information will be provided, according to the department.
The deaths come as cases in the state have surpassed 11,000 for a total of 11,234, including 193 hospitalizations, MDHHS data shows.
MDHHS added that cyclosporiasis is typically not a life-threatening illness and that deaths are uncommon in the U.S.
Federal health officials have so far linked cases in Michigan and eight other states to shredded iceberg lettuce served at some Taco Bell restaurants.
Taylor Farms, the supplier of the lettuce, issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico. Consumers are being advised to throw out or return any iceberg lettuce.
Taco Bell said last month that it is no longer using lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico at any of its restaurants.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) wrote on its website that it “is aware of two cyclosporiasis-related deaths in people with underlying health conditions from Michigan as part of this outbreak. CDC will update its website to include laboratory confirmed cases, hospitalizations and deaths.”
The CDC has previously said it is investigating other outbreaks and illnesses of cyclosporiasis nationally that are unrelated to the nine-state outbreak.
Since May 1, cases of cyclosporiasis have topped 18,000 in 45 states, according to data updated by the CDC on Wednesday.
There are at least 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, including 423 hospitalizations, the data shows.
The CDC said it can take up to six weeks to determine if a sick person should be counted in the agency’s tally, meaning nationally reported cases may be lower than state totals.
Meanwhile, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) published data last week showing a “sharp rise” in cyclosporiasis infections among travelers returning from Mexico.
Between April 30 and July 15, 67 cases have been reported among returning travelers in England, Wales and Scotland. Comparatively, an annual average of 93 cases has been recorded between 2022 and 2025.
UKHSA said it is advising all travelers to take precautions when traveling abroad including “maintaining good food and water hygiene to reduce their risk of infection.”
Cyclospora, the parasite that causes infection, usually spreads through food or water contaminated with feces, according to the CDC.
Foodborne outbreaks of cyclosporiasis have been linked to various types of imported fresh produce, such as raspberries, basil, snow peas, mesclun lettuce and cilantro, the CDC says.
The most common symptom of cyclosporiasis is watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the CDC. Other symptoms nay include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or bloating.

sources.news_title: Nurses Chase Cyclospora, Aided by Interviews, Fast-Food Receipts — And the Messy Details
sources.text:
Nurses Chase Cyclospora, Aided by Interviews, Fast-Food Receipts — And the Messy Details
More than 900 people in Washtenaw County, Michigan, have been sickened with cyclosporiasis since mid-June. Linda Kim, a public health nurse, has called more than 100 of them. Almost everyone has said the same thing: It’s excruciating, and one of the worst illnesses they’ve experienced.
But on a Wednesday in July, she called one man who said he wouldn’t mind having it again, actually.
“You’re enjoying the weight loss?” Kim said, laughing as she took notes in a small conference room at the Washtenaw County Health Department building, just outside Ann Arbor. “Well, I’m glad to hear that. At least you got something good out of it!”
Normally, Kim’s supposed to be working downstairs in the clinic, where families wait in gray plastic chairs in the lobby for free or low-cost immunizations. But she hasn’t been there in months.
In March, Kim was transferred to a different department to help deal with a measles outbreak that sickened seven people in the county, five of them children. It was an all-hands-on-deck situation; everyone worked overtime. The state issued an advisory urging families in Washtenaw and surrounding counties to get babies 6 months or older vaccinated ahead of schedule, if possible.
The contact-tracing calls for measles could be contentious, Kim said. People were suspicious, asking her how she knew they had tested positive, or why they should give her any information.
“People were like, ‘Oh, you’re just trying to restrict my life,’ or ‘You’re just trying to get information out of me and get me in trouble,’” she said. “It’s like, no, we’re actually not doing that at all.”
As she tried to explain to them, tracing the spread of the highly contagious virus and publicizing possible exposure sites was an effort to “keep it contained, so it doesn’t become something huge.”
The county’s measles outbreak ended in late May. Then in June, reports of cyclosporiasis cases started pouring in — more than 11,000 so far in Michigan, including two deaths. Both people who died had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” the state health department said on its website Aug. 3. Health officials aren’t providing more details, department spokesperson Lynn Sutfin said in an email, but are stressing that cyclosporiasis generally isn’t life-threatening and that deaths from it are uncommon in the U.S.
Kim said the cyclosporiasis surveillance has been very different from her experience with the measles outbreak. Now, people seem eager to divulge even the most graphic details, such as “pooping their beds, and, like, putting down towels and it’s not enough.”
Since she’s a nurse, such confessions don’t faze her, she said. Still, staffers have hundreds of these calls to make, so they try to keep each conversation under an hour.
But foodborne illness investigations are complex. Especially for this parasite, cyclospora. Symptoms can take as long as two weeks to appear after people have eaten contaminated food. And no one remembers what they ate two weeks ago, public health staffers said.
The interview process can be extremely detailed. Kim and her colleagues ask people to pull up their restaurant receipts, scroll through purchases on their grocery store apps, even try to recall details such as the exact brand of bagged salad mix they bought, or the type of taco they got at Taco Bell.
“Is that the crunchy one or the soft one?” Kim asked on a recent call, typing on a laptop decorated with cat and vaccine-themed stickers.
Kim has been working with the health department for two years, a period defined by federal funding cuts.
Laina Stebbins, a spokesperson for the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, said the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts to public health grants eliminated a contract between the state health department and 44 of the state’s 45 local departments that funded 123 full-time employees.
Those cuts also affected the state’s disease surveillance labs, “reducing funding for equipment maintenance contracts, data modernization, and the ability to innovate laboratory processes during emerging disease response,” Stebbins said.
Some of that funding was restored after Michigan won a temporary restraining order against the Trump administration. But Washtenaw’s health department still had to scale back some disease surveillance and outbreak response work. Currently, employees who leave or retire aren’t replaced, except for those on the nursing team, which is hiring but still understaffed.
The county’s Health Equity Council, which aims to reduce health disparities, including in mental health, was shuttered suddenly in early 2025. Nearly a year later, it resumed its work, with funding at least through this September.
An employee from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had been stationed at the department. During the funding chaos, the worker was fired, then rehired, then furloughed.
The federal response to cyclosporiasis has felt frustratingly slow, according to Christina Zilke, a nursing supervisor at the Washtenaw health department.
“It took them forever to say that this was lettuce, and fast-food restaurants were taking it off the shelves before the CDC ever said what it was,” she said.
During a July 14 press call, the deputy director of the CDC’s Division of Foodborne, Waterborne, and Environmental Diseases, Gwen Biggerstaff, said it’s not unusual for it to take a long time to identify a specific source for cyclosporiasis — if it’s identified at all. That’s partly due to the lag time between exposure and the appearance of symptoms, and the complexity of tracing this particular parasite.
Meanwhile, Zilke’s been stocking the coffee station and bringing in pizza, trying to keep up staff morale. It’s not a reward, she said. “It’s more like: ‘Here’s some food for survival. Here’s a break so you don’t quit.’”
Kim, for her part, remains enthusiastic about the job but said it’s been a surreal introduction to a public health career — first measles, now cyclospora.
“If nationally they don’t know what’s going on, how are we locally expected to know what’s going on?” she said. “And also just frustrating to be, like, ‘Wow, I don’t think even our government knows how important public health is.’”
But there’s no time to dwell. She has to move on to the next call, as soon as she can wrap up this one. She gives each person her work number, so people can call or text with any follow-up questions.

One in three Britons hit by travel bug as cyclosporiasis outbreak turns deadly in the US
Two people have died in a US cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to contaminated lettuce
Latest
Michigan's health department confirmed on Monday that two individuals have died from cyclosporiasis, representing the first fatalities linked to America's largest recorded outbreak of the parasitic intestinal disease.
"According to medical records, both individuals had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration," a spokesperson for the Michigan Department of Health & Human Services stated.
The department declined to release further details about the deceased, emphasising that cyclosporiasis is "generally not a life-threatening illness" and that deaths from the condition remain rare in the United States.
The US Department of Health and Human Services acknowledged it was aware of the Michigan fatalities, as the outbreak continues to spread alarm across the country.
Two patients with conditions impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration have died
|GETTY
By Monday, Michigan had recorded 11,234 cases connected to the outbreak, a rise of 461 since the previous Friday update. Some 193 people have required hospital treatment.
Wayne County bears the heaviest burden, with 1,379 confirmed infections. Those between 30 and 39 years of age have proved most susceptible, comprising 2,216 of the reported cases.
An investigation by the US Food and Drug Administration has traced the outbreak to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms, a privately owned company with operations in central Mexico. Authorities have not, however, ruled out additional sources of contamination.
American consumers have responded by avoiding certain restaurant chains and reducing lettuce purchases, as the multi-state crisis sows widespread confusion about which foods remain safe to eat.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS:
Across the nation, the CDC had logged 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases as of 28 July, with upwards of 11,500 suspected infections still awaiting confirmation. The outbreak now spans nine states.
Former CDC officials and food safety specialists have warned that reductions to federal health agencies have hampered the government's capacity to tackle foodborne disease outbreaks effectively.
Wade Syers, a food safety specialist at Michigan State University Extension, said: "This development highlights the importance of identifying the source of the outbreak and preventing additional illnesses."
The CDC's surveillance figures capture only laboratory-confirmed infections, whilst individual state health departments may additionally report probable cases, which accounts for the discrepancy between state and national tallies.
The outbreak's focus on contaminated produce carries resonance for British travellers, too. Research from Saga Travel Insurance reveals that more than a third of UK holidaymakers — 36 per cent — have suffered from so-called "travel tummy" within the past year alone.
Symptoms typically include severe diarrhoea and nausea
|GETTY
Dr Nick Burr, a gastroenterologist at healthcare provider LivingCare, said: "Traveller's diarrhoea is usually caused by bacteria, most commonly E. coli, picked up from contaminated food or water, particularly in parts of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Central or South America."
Nearly half of those surveyed attributed their stomach troubles to local cuisine. Dr Burr identified untreated water, ice cubes, buffets, undercooked meat and food left in warm conditions as typical culprits.
Dehydration poses the gravest risk, particularly in hot climates — a danger underscored by the Michigan fatalities, where dehydration was cited as a contributing factor.

Susan Ringler Cerniglia, spokesperson for the Washtenaw County Health Department, where 875 cases have been reported, said: ‘We have one clear implicated food, but it doesn’t explain everything.’

sources.news_title: Michigan Confirms First Two Deaths in Record Cyclospora Outbreak as CDC Tally Still Shows None
sources.text:
Michigan Confirms First Two Deaths in Record Cyclospora Outbreak as CDC Tally Still Shows None
Michigan health officials confirmed on Monday that two people have died after becoming ill with cyclosporiasis, the first deaths reported in connection with a parasite outbreak that has produced more than 18,000 confirmed and suspected illnesses across the United States since the start of May.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said medical records show both individuals had significant underlying health conditions that may have been affected by cyclosporiasis and dehydration. The department said no additional information about the two cases will be released.
An FDA spokesperson said both people became ill before the Taylor Farms de Mexico recall of iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico.
The disclosure changes the risk picture in a specific way. Until Monday, federal and state agencies had described cyclosporiasis as an illness that is unpleasant and persistent but rarely dangerous. MDHHS has not withdrawn that characterization; it noted alongside the announcement that death from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States. What has changed is that the outbreak is now large enough, and has reached enough medically vulnerable people, that a rare outcome has occurred twice in one state.
The First Fatalities in a Record Season
Michigan has reported 11,234 cyclosporiasis cases since its outbreak investigation period began in early May, according to the state dashboard. Of those patients, 193 had been hospitalized as of the most recent weekly update. In a typical year, the state records roughly 50 cases, meaning the current total is more than 200 times its usual annual burden. Wayne County has reported the most cases, and adults in their thirties account for the largest share.
The national picture is also without precedent. CDC surveillance shows 6,707 laboratory-confirmed, domestically acquired cases since May 1, plus more than 11,500 additional cases that are not yet laboratory confirmed or that require further investigation, many of them from Michigan and Ohio. Cases have been reported in 45 states. The agency has counted 423 hospitalizations among laboratory-confirmed patients and, as of that update, no deaths.
The worst previous year on record was 2019, when roughly 4,700 confirmed and suspected illnesses were reported nationally; the laboratory-confirmed domestic count that year was 2,408. By either measure, this season has already surpassed it.
Federal investigators have linked a nine-state cluster — Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia — to shredded iceberg lettuce from a single supplier served at Taco Bell locations. That cluster accounts for at least 1,947 laboratory-confirmed illnesses and at least 98 hospitalizations. Taco Bell said it completed removal of the affected lettuce from its restaurants, and Taylor Farms recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico the same day, later suspending sourcing from the region for the rest of the growing season.
One caveat belongs with that finding. The FDA's traceback converged on a single supplier, but the agency has not reported a confirmed positive product sample, and an earlier reported positive test was retracted. The FDA is also investigating at least five additional cyclosporiasis outbreaks whose sources have not been identified.
Federal and State Counts Are Not Telling the Same Story
Readers checking official numbers this week will find two different answers, and the discrepancy is worth understanding rather than dismissing.
The CDC's laboratory-confirmed table does not reflect any deaths, and its national case total sits well below the combined figures reported by states. That is a function of reporting mechanics rather than disagreement. The agency counts only laboratory-confirmed cases with international travel ruled out and publishes weekly; it has said confirmation can take as long as six weeks. State dashboards include probable cases and update far more frequently.
For anyone tracking this outbreak in August, the practical implication is that state health department pages are the more current source and the federal figure is the more conservative one. Michigan updates case counts each weekday morning and posts hospitalization and detailed outbreak data on Thursdays.
Officials have flagged a second limitation. Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, Michigan's chief medical executive, told NBC News that some health systems have restricted testing to patients who are severely ill or immunocompromised, because of laboratory backlogs and supply limits. She said that makes it harder to judge whether the apparent slowdown is real, and that she does not know whether a single product recall explains it. Counts that fall partly because fewer people are tested are not the same as an outbreak ending. The state has also reported that a batch of roughly 475 cases added in late July reflected delayed laboratory processing rather than new illness.
Michigan has seen two distinct waves of illness, one in late June and one in early July. Barbara Kowalcyk, who directs the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, has attributed that pattern to contaminated product arriving in two separate batches, and has noted that ongoing contamination of irrigation or processing water would keep an outbreak going.
Dehydration, Not the Parasite Itself, Is the Immediate Danger
Cyclospora cayetanensis is a microscopic parasite spread through food or water contaminated with feces. It does not pass directly from person to person. The most common symptom is frequent, sometimes explosive watery diarrhea, along with loss of appetite, weight loss, bloating, nausea, and fatigue. Symptoms usually begin about a week after exposure, with a range of roughly two days to two weeks.
Cyclosporiasis is treated with the antibiotic combination trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and symptoms often improve within days of starting treatment. Many otherwise healthy people recover without treatment, though untreated symptoms can appear to clear and then return repeatedly over weeks.
The mechanism behind the two deaths appears to involve fluid loss rather than the infection itself. Severe, prolonged diarrhea and vomiting can produce dangerous dehydration, which is far more consequential for people whose kidneys, hearts or immune systems are already compromised. That is the group guidance points to most directly: older adults, people receiving cancer treatment or taking immunosuppressive drugs, people with chronic kidney or cardiovascular disease, and infants.
Neither MDHHS nor the CDC has released case-fatality figures, and neither has revised its assessment that cyclosporiasis is not typically life-threatening. Both statements can be true at once. A rare outcome becomes visible when the denominator grows into the tens of thousands.
Steps for Households Still Buying Summer Produce
Recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce should be discarded or returned. Beyond that specific product, no single item explains the majority of cases, which means prevention advice remains general.
MDHHS has advised buying whole heads of lettuce rather than prewashed bagged lettuce or salad mixes, discarding the outer two to three layers of leaves, and washing the inner leaves under running water. For greens that can be cooked, cooking is the safest option. Rinsing reduces risk but does not eliminate it, and the CDC has warned that chemically disinfecting or sanitizing produce may not fully eliminate the parasite. Handwashing before food preparation remains standard guidance.
If a household member has watery diarrhea lasting more than a few days, asking a clinician for cyclospora testing is worth doing, because the parasite is not detected unless testing for it is ordered. Signs that warrant prompt medical evaluation include very little urine output, dizziness on standing, confusion, an inability to keep fluids down, or bloody stools. Anyone who is pregnant, immunocompromised, or caring for an older adult should seek guidance sooner rather than later. Local health departments can direct uninsured patients toward lower-cost testing. This article is general information and not a diagnosis.
Cases of cyclosporiasis typically rise from the start of May through the end of August, according to the CDC. The agency updates national surveillance weekly.
The newest confirmed fact is that two Michigan residents with significant underlying conditions have died in connection with this outbreak. Those most affected are medically vulnerable adults in the hardest-hit states. The most reasonable action is treating persistent watery diarrhea as something worth a phone call rather than something to wait out. The central uncertainty is whether the recalled lettuce explains the full outbreak or whether other contaminated products remain in circulation.
Frequently Asked Questions
What exactly did Michigan announce? MDHHS confirmed two deaths connected to the state's cyclosporiasis outbreak. Medical records show both people had significant underlying health conditions that may have been affected by cyclosporiasis and dehydration. No further identifying details are being released.
Are these the first cyclosporiasis deaths in the United States? They are the first deaths reported in connection with this outbreak, and officials describe deaths from cyclosporiasis in the US as uncommon. The CDC's laboratory-confirmed surveillance table had not been updated to reflect them as of its most recent weekly posting.
How many people have been infected? Michigan reports 11,234 cases, with 193 hospitalizations as of the latest weekly update. Nationally, the CDC reported 6,707 laboratory-confirmed domestic cases since May 1 and more than 11,500 additional unresolved cases across 45 states.
Which foods have been linked to the outbreak? Shredded iceberg lettuce from central Mexico supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico has been tied to a nine-state cluster and was recalled in July. Other clusters have no identified source, and no positive product sample has been confirmed. Past outbreaks have involved raspberries, bagged salads, cilantro and basil.
Who is most at risk of serious illness? Older adults, people who are immunocompromised, and people with chronic kidney or heart conditions face the greatest risk, primarily because prolonged diarrhea can cause severe dehydration. Most otherwise healthy adults recover, and antibiotic treatment shortens the illness.
Does washing produce remove the parasite? Rinsing reduces risk but does not eliminate it, and sanitizing rinses may not either. Michigan officials recommend buying whole heads of lettuce, discarding outer leaves, washing thoroughly, and cooking greens when possible.
When should someone see a doctor? Watery diarrhea lasting more than a few days warrants a call to a clinician, and cyclospora testing should be requested specifically. Signs of dehydration such as minimal urination, dizziness, or confusion require prompt evaluation.

sources.news_title: Michigan Reports First Deaths In Parasite Outbreak
sources.text:
Two people in Michigan have died in connection with the state's sprawling cyclosporiasis outbreak, health officials said Monday, marking the first reported deaths tied to an unusually severe nationwide parasite season that has sickened tens of thousands of Americans since May.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said the deaths were identified as part of an outbreak that has now sickened 11,234 people statewide, with 193 hospitalizations reported as of July 30. The department said medical records showed both individuals "had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration," and that no further information about the cases, including their identities, would be released. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed on its website that it "is aware of two cyclosporiasis-related deaths in people with underlying health conditions from Michigan as part of this outbreak," noting that death resulting from the illness is uncommon in the United States.
Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis, a microscopic parasite found in human feces that can contaminate fresh produce or water. Symptoms typically appear one to two weeks after exposure and include watery, often "explosive" diarrhea, along with severe abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea, fatigue and significant weight loss; some patients experience 20 to 30 bouts of diarrhea a day, according to Dr. Anurag Malani, an infectious disease specialist and vice chief of medical staff at Trinity Health Ann Arbor Hospital. Left untreated, symptoms can persist or recur intermittently for weeks or months, and the resulting dehydration from frequent diarrhea and vomiting can itself become dangerous, particularly for people with existing health conditions, according to Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. The illness is typically treated with the antibiotic Bactrim, though many people with healthy immune systems recover without treatment.
Nationally, the CDC has recorded roughly 18,000 confirmed and probable cyclosporiasis cases since May across 45 states, compared with an average of about 3,000 cases in a typical year. Michigan's outbreak, the largest in the country this season, has been linked along with outbreaks in eight other states to shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico, which was used in salads at Taco Bell locations nationwide; Taylor Farms de Mexico issued a voluntary recall of the affected lettuce on July 17, and both the supplier and Taco Bell have since removed it from their supply chains. A separate, unrelated outbreak tied to Del Monte vegetable trays sold at Kwik Trip gas stations across Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Michigan has sickened 227 people and hospitalized seven, with no deaths reported in that cluster. An FDA spokesperson told NBC News that the two people who died in Michigan had fallen ill before Taylor Farms issued its recall, according to data provided by the state health department, though federal officials cautioned that finding applies specifically to the Michigan-centered outbreak and the eight other states linked to it, not to cyclosporiasis cases nationwide.
That Michigan health officials confirmed two deaths while explicitly declining to release further details, including whether the victims had consumed the recalled lettuce, suggests the state is prioritizing patient privacy over providing a fuller public accounting of how the fatalities specifically connect to the broader outbreak's identified source. The finding that both deaths occurred before Taylor Farms' recall took effect indicates the July 17 action, whatever its effectiveness going forward, could not have prevented these particular cases, a distinction that matters for evaluating how quickly the outbreak's source was identified relative to when illnesses were already occurring. The stark gap between this year's roughly 18,000 national cases and the typical annual average of 3,000 illustrates how significantly this cyclosporiasis season has outpaced historical patterns, even before accounting for the additional, unrelated Del Monte-linked cluster affecting several of the same states.
Attention in the coming days is likely to center on whether additional deaths are identified as Michigan and other affected states continue their outbreak investigations, and on whether health officials release any further detail about the specific circumstances of the two fatalities. Continued monitoring of case counts across the 45 affected states, the effectiveness of the Taylor Farms recall in curbing new infections, and whether any additional food sources are identified in the ongoing investigation are expected to remain relevant threads as the outbreak continues.

“Two deaths have been identified as part of the cyclosporiasis outbreak affecting Michigan. No additional information will be provided on these two cases,” according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.

Some cyclosporiasis infections may improve on their own, but without treatment, symptoms may last a month or longer, and persistent diarrhea can make it difficult to stay hydrated. Dehydration from frequent bouts of diarrhea can also cause severe illness.
Cases of cyclosporiasis are known to rise during spring and summer months in the US, with a typical season running from the start of May through the end of August, according to the CDC. But case counts are particularly high this year.
The CDC has identified more than 18,000 cases of domestic cyclosporiasis this season; 6,707 cases are confirmed, and about 11,500 others are undergoing further laboratory testing and analysis to determine whether the illness was acquired in the US.
Multiple clusters of cyclosporiasis cases are being investigated this year by the US Food and Drug Administration in collaboration with the CDC and state partners, including the particularly large multistate outbreak centered in the Midwest.

The illness is transmitted through a microscopic parasite called cyclospora, which is spread through food or water that has been contaminated by fecal matter. The FDA recalled iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms (a Taco Bell supplier), for example, after identifying it as a potential source of one of the recent outbreaks.
How to Prevent Cyclosporiasis?
As concerns grow following the recent deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is urging people to take proactive measures to prevent the spread of cyclosporiasis.
CDC officials say there are five main ways to prevent the spread of cyclosporiasis at home, with specific products you can use to kill any contamination.
1. Wash Hands With Soap and Water When Handling Product
The CDC says it’s important to not just wash your hands before handling or preparing raw fruits and vegetables, but to also wash your hands afterward.

sources.news_title: First deaths in Cyclospora outbreak reported by Michigan
sources.text:
The nationwide outbreak of infections from the Cyclospora parasite has turned deadly with Michigan reporting two deaths over the weekend.
A statement from the state health department said both of the patients had underlying health conditions, but that dehydration from their Cyclospora infections was the cause of death. As of today, Michigan is reporting 11,234 patients with at least 193 having been hospitalized. As of July 31 the state had 10,773 patients.
Ohio’s count is more than 4,000, Missouri has more than 1,000 and there are several other states with patient counts in the hundreds. North Carolina reports more than 700 patients and is saying that the infections may be related to parsley or cilantro, but the state has not said where the leafy greens were grown or what brand they were sold under.
The Centers for Disease Control has not updated its patient count yet this week. The agency is investigating several outbreaks but is giving special attention to one that involves nine states. The CDC’s report last week showed 1,947 patients in the nine-state outbreak that covers Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Interviews with people sickened with cyclosporiasis in this outbreak indicate that many in those states ate at Taco Bell restaurants and ate iceberg lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms de Mexico. That lettuce has since been recalled. Many of the patients became sick before the lettuce was recalled. However, some patients continue to report illness onset after the recalled lettuce was past its expiration date.
As of this week the agency was reporting that since May 1 there have been 6,707 domestically acquired, lab-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, and an additional 11,500 are awaiting confirmation or need more investigation. Those numbers include patients in 45 states. A source of the parasite for the outbreaks has not yet been determined.
“CDC's surveillance updates do not include probable cases. State data may include probable and confirmed cases, resulting in higher case counts than what CDC reports,” according to the CDC update posted early last week.
As of Friday, the total from state reports was more than 20,000.
About Cyclospora
Food contaminated with the microscopic Cyclospora parasite does not look, smell or taste bad.
Anyone who has developed symptoms of Cyclospora infection, and has reason to believe they have been exposed to the parasite, should seek medical attention. Specific tests are required and antibiotics are used to fight the parasite.
Cyclospora infection can cause severe abdominal pain, intense watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, body aches, and fatigue. Symptoms can develop between two and 14 days after exposure. Though symptoms can be severe enough to send people to the hospital, it's rare for people to die from Cyclospora infections.
Symptoms can last for a month or more and can reoccur for several more months if not treated.
Cyclospora is a type of protozoa, which is a single-celled organism. It is transmitted when people somehow ingest contaminated feces, typically through contaminated food or water. It can be spread only through human waste, unlike E. coli and salmonella, which can also be spread from animal fecal matter.
Previous U.S. outbreaks of cyclosporiasis have been linked to various types of fresh produce, including lettuce, basil, cilantro, mesclun lettuce, raspberries, and snow peas.
Food safety experts say there's no evidence that washing the produce will remove the parasite because it becomes embedded in the flesh of the produce.

sources.text: Michigan has reported the first two known U.S. deaths connected to the nation’s largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak, according to state health officials. Federal investigators have linked part of the outbreak to recalled iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants in nine states, while authorities continue searching for other possible sources. More than 11,000 cases have been reported in Michigan, and symptoms can include severe diarrhea, nausea and dehydration.

State officials reported 11,234 cases as of August 3, an increase of 461 since July 31, with 193 hospitalizations recorded as of July 30, far above Michigan’s typical annual total of about 50 cases.
📺 DETAIL: Health officials said the illness is generally not life-threatening, but dehydration and other complications can be severe, particularly for vulnerable people. The outbreak, first identified in Monroe County in late June, has spread to 70 counties, with Oakland and Wayne counties each reporting more than 1,000 cases and several others exceeding 300. Canadian health officials in Ontario’s Windsor-Essex region have warned residents traveling to Michigan after identifying 24 cases this year, with many linked to recent travel across the border. Investigators believe lettuce or salad greens are the likely source of the outbreak, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has linked one cluster to a Taco Bell lettuce supplier, prompting Taylor Farms to voluntarily recall iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico. Multiple outbreak clusters remain under investigation nationwide.
🎯 IMPACT: The outbreak has prompted public health warnings, reduced consumer confidence in produce, and led todeclining lettuce sales. Health officials are urging thorough washing of fruits and vegetables and caution when consuming raw produce.
📈 DATA: Michigan has seen an unprecedented spike in cases, with over 11,234 reported as of August 3, compared to an annual average of 50 cases. Notably, the CDC’s national tally excludes probablecases, focusing only on laboratory-confirmed infections.
📺 FLASHBACK: Previous outbreaks of cyclosporiasis in the U.S. have often been linked to imported produce, suggesting possible public health benefits from buying American.

DETROIT — Two people have died in the cyclospora outbreak in Michigan, state health officials announced Monday, the first deaths confirmed in the U.S. related to the microscopic parasite.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said both people had underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by the intestinal illness and dehydration. The department said it would not provide additional information about the deaths.
Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.
The CDC says the illness, called cyclosporiasis, is rarely deadly.
The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water.
Dr. Joel Kammeyer, the division chief of infectious diseases at Wayne State University and the Detroit Medical Center, called the deaths a “tragedy” but noted that despite thousands of cyclosporiasis cases, only two people have died.
“For someone who comes into an urgent care and cyclosporiasis is their only issue, it’s relatively easy to treat,” Kammeyer said. But for people who are struggling with other illnesses, he said, “it stands to reason that there are some patients that might not be able to withstand the dehydration that can come with severe cyclosporiasis.”
Cyclosporiasis is less common than other foodborne illnesses, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source and, for years, few U.S. cyclospora outbreaks were reported. But the number started rising about a decade ago, with a particularly notable spike in 2018 and 2019.
Previously, 2019 saw the most reported U.S. cyclosporiasis cases, with about 4,700.
The CDC said it is aware of more than 18,000 confirmed or suspected cases in the current surge. But CDC numbers can lag state reports, which suggest the number is more than 20,000 nationwide.
Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in nine states as a source of the widespread outbreak . As of late July, the number of cases linked to the lettuce was 1,947, including at least 98 people who had to be hospitalized, according to the CDC.
The agency has said other “brands, restaurants, retailers, or distribution channels” could be tied to the outbreak as the investigation continues.

sources.news_title: Taylor Farms’ Shifting Words on Cyclospora Outbreak Raise Fresh Questions About 2013 Lessons and Testing Limits
sources.text:
Bill Marler has spent decades building legal cases on corporate statements issued during foodborne outbreaks. He treats them as evidence. What a company says publicly, and how it revises those words over days and weeks, reveals what it knew and when.
This summer’s Cyclospora outbreak linked to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce from central Mexico has produced more than 1,600 confirmed cases across dozens of states. Hospitalizations exceed 140. Two deaths have been reported in Michigan. The numbers dwarf typical seasonal figures. Last year at this time, CDC had recorded just 249 domestically acquired cases.
CDC’s investigation update from July 24, 2026 states that epidemiologic and traceback data continue to show iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico contaminated with Cyclospora and making people sick. The agency expanded the outbreak to nine states. Taco Bell locations in several of them served the shredded product.
Taylor Farms issued a voluntary recall on July 17. The company pulled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico. It later suspended production and sourcing from the region entirely. Yet its public explanations have changed four times in sixteen days. The revisions, documented in detail by food safety attorney Bill Marler, omit key admissions from the original statement. They never address what, if anything, changed at the Doctor Mora, Guanajuato plant after a major 2013 outbreak.
The company’s statements evolved rapidly while core questions went unanswered.
The original July 17 statement began with concern for those sickened and their families. It acknowledged that trust in produce takes decades to earn and is easily lost. It tied the recall directly to information provided by FDA the previous day. And it included a detail that vanished from every subsequent version. FDA’s traceback, the statement said, pointed to a specific independent farm representing less than one percent of U.S. iceberg supply.
One day later, FDA announced a positive Cyclospora test on a product sample. The next day, July 19, the agency retracted it as a false positive. Taylor Farms updated its statement that same day. Sympathy for victims moved down the page. The recall shifted to past tense and was framed as an abundance of caution. The reference to the specific farm disappeared. No note explained the removal.
Marler’s analysis on his blog tracks each iteration. By July 24 the page led with the company’s $200 million annual spend on food safety protocols. It announced suspension of central Mexico sourcing since July 18 and a third-party review. The earlier claim of an FDA apology was simply gone.
On July 30 Taylor Farms launched a dedicated Cyclospora information hub. A July 31 revision added West Virginia to the list of states receiving recalled product. The distribution paragraph on the same page still omitted it. West Virginia sits among the nine states in the federal investigation.
But words are only part of the picture. The 2013 record looms large. That year Cyclospora sickened 631 people in 25 states. Iowa and Nebraska accounted for 239 cases tied to salad mix from Taylor Farms de Mexico served at Olive Garden and Red Lobster restaurants. FDA’s environmental assessment examined the processing plant and five ranches. Investigators tested roughly 835 samples, including more than 269 human fecal specimens. None yielded the parasite. The assessment began five weeks after the last illness.
The agency’s recommendations carried weight. Taylor Farms should determine whether Cyclospora represented a reasonably likely food safety hazard in the Guanajuato growing region. If so, it should re-evaluate the wash step. The company suspended shipments August 9, 2013, and resumed August 25 after FDA reviewed its new product sampling plan for the parasite.
Thirteen years later, that sampling plan’s results have never been published. Taylor Farms’ current hub states that approximately 2,000 samples taken in central Mexico since May returned zero positives for Cyclospora. As of July 24, FDA had no confirmed positive product tests. The company uses FDA-validated methods described in the Bacteriological Analytical Manual chapters 19b and 19c.
Yet detection rates for these methods vary. One study cited by Marler put recovery at 93 percent under ideal conditions. Modeling suggests real-world performance closer to 30 percent. Negative tests, even in large numbers, do not prove absence when the organism is hardy, adheres to produce surfaces, and resists standard washing. Cyclospora oocysts survive months in water or soil. No kill step exists for ready-to-eat lettuce.
FDA’s fact sheet for farmers lists Mexico among countries where cyclosporiasis is endemic. The preventive controls rule under FSMA requires hazard analysis. If a processor deems Cyclospora reasonably likely, it must implement and verify preventive controls with records. Taylor Farms’ hub describes rigorous ranch inspections and adjacent land reviews. A public swimming resort sits roughly 800 feet from the Doctor Mora facility. Satellite images show it operating years before the 2013 assessment.
The company has not explained how its hazard analysis evolved after 2013. It has not detailed verification data from the sampling plan FDA reviewed before reopening the plant. It has not addressed whether the wash step was re-evaluated as recommended. And it has not reconciled 2,000 negative tests with an outbreak that federal data link to its product.
Recent developments add pressure. U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal requested records from Taylor Farms concerning its communications with the White House and FDA, according to a report in Food Poisoning Bulletin on August 3, 2026. At least 13 lawsuits have been filed, including one by a Warren, Michigan woman against both Taylor Farms and Taco Bell, the Detroit News reported today.
Two deaths tied to the outbreak involved individuals with underlying conditions. Their illness onsets occurred before the July 17 recall. HHS noted the timing in statements covered on social media and news outlets today.
Taylor Farms is no stranger to outbreaks. Its onions were linked to a 2024 E. coli event tied to McDonald’s Quarter Pounders that sickened over 100, hospitalized dozens and caused one death. FDA inspections afterward found sanitation lapses at a Colorado plant. In 2015 a celery-onion mix from the company was recalled in connection with an E. coli outbreak in Costco chicken salad.
The 2013 Cyclospora event itself was not isolated. Texas cases that summer traced to cilantro from a different producer. More than 100 additional illnesses went unexplained. Yet the Iowa and Nebraska cluster pointed clearly to Taylor Farms de Mexico salad mix.
Produce safety has improved since then. FSMA brought new rules. Testing technology advanced. Traceback systems grew more sophisticated. Still, Cyclospora remains difficult to detect and control in leafy greens grown in regions where it circulates. Irrigation water, worker hygiene, and adjacent land use all matter. So does transparency when problems surface.
Taylor Farms’ hub emphasizes its audited protocols and commitment to safety. It reports commissioning independent experts for a full review. Those steps matter. But the evolving statements and persistent silence on post-2013 changes leave gaps. Regulators, lawmakers, plaintiffs’ attorneys and the public want specifics. What did the hazard analysis conclude? What preventive controls were applied? What did the 2,000 tests actually verify, given known method limitations? How was the swimming resort evaluated in adjacent land reviews?
Answers could clarify whether this outbreak reflects a known hazard that slipped through controls or something new. They could inform prevention across the industry. Without them, the revisions read as damage control rather than accountability. And the questions first raised in 2013 remain open in 2026.
Marler closed his August 3 post with a challenge. The company has rewritten its message repeatedly. It still has not said what changed at that plant after 2013 or why two thousand negative tests should mean anything. Until it does, the statements themselves stand as the clearest public record.

sources.text:
Michigan reports first US deaths in cyclosporiasis outbreak
The outbreak of the intestinal illness has been linked to iceberg lettuce from some operations in central Mexico, but authorities are still seeking other potential sources.
A cyclosporiasis outbreak that has grown into the largest on record in the United States has caused its first known deaths, two people in Michigan, the state's health department said on Monday (Aug 3).
Cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness caused by the Cyclospora parasite, is generally not life-threatening. Michigan, citing medical records, said the two who died had significant underlying health conditions that may have been affected by the disease and related dehydration.
An FDA investigation linked the outbreak, now in nine states, to iceberg lettuce sourced from privately held Taylor Farms operations in central Mexico and served at Yum Brands-owned Taco Bell. The lettuce has been recalled, but authorities are still seeking other potential sources.
Epidemiologists suspect multiple outbreaks, and it was not immediately clear whether the people who died were sickened from Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants, or from another yet to be identified source.
US cyclosporiasis cases have climbed to record levels this year, with the current outbreak among the largest caused by foodborne illness in recent US history.
It has also hurt consumer confidence, lowering lettuce sales and visits to restaurant chains such as Sweetgreen and Chipotle.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), whose surveillance lags state reporting by several weeks, has recorded 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases nationwide as of Jul 28, along with more than 11,500 suspected cases not yet confirmed through laboratory testing. State counts run higher because the CDC excludes probable cases.
MICHIGAN HARDEST HIT
Michigan, the hardest-hit state, has recorded 11,234 cases as of Monday, up 461 from Friday, with 193 hospitalised, health department data shows.
The large number of cases, gaps in reporting and people's difficulty recalling what they ate have made it harder for investigators to determine which foods, beyond Taylor Farms lettuce, may have contributed to the outbreak, local Michigan health officials said.
"We have one clear implicated food, but it doesn't explain everything," said Susan Ringler Cerniglia, spokesperson for the Washtenaw County Health Department, where 875 cases have been reported.
Mixed messaging from the US Department of Health and Human Services had also complicated the response, she said. Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has said the outbreak is under control.
"Leadership is saying things that don't really fit with what the data is telling us, and that's very, very problematic," Ringler Cerniglia said. "The secretary is saying this is under control and it's all good while you have case counts exploding."
HHS said on Monday it was aware of the deaths.
Michigan's Wayne County, which includes Detroit, has the highest number of cases at 1,379, state data showed.
Cases have been rising steadily across the US in recent weeks, according to the CDC. Symptoms include severe diarrhoea, which can lead to dehydration, nausea and other gastrointestinal issues.
HEALTH AGENCY CUTS MAY HAMPER RESPONSE
Former CDC officials and food safety experts say cuts across federal health agencies have complicated the government's ability to respond to foodborne outbreaks.
Cyclospora is harder to track than many foodborne pathogens because, unlike bacteria, it cannot be grown in the lab or easily genome-mapped to trace an outbreak, said Dr Paul Bollyky, a professor of infectious disease at Stanford Medicine.
That makes standard epidemiology and contact tracing more difficult and labour-intensive, he said, work not made any easier with understaffing at public health departments.
"It certainly doesn't help matters to have underfunded or understaffed public health departments," Bollyky said, adding that budget cuts and turnover at the CDC would make outbreaks like this harder to trace and control.
The scale of the outbreak raises broader questions about the safety of the US food supply, he said.
"Anytime you have over 10,000 people infected with a foodborne pathogen, you do have to wonder whether this is a canary in the coal mine."

Two deaths in Michigan mark the first fatalities in the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in US history, linked to contaminated lettuce
Two people have died in Michigan after contracting cyclosporiasis, marking the first known fatalities in the largest outbreak of the parasitic illness ever recorded in the United States. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) confirmed the deaths on 3 August 2026, as the statewide case count climbed to 11,234.
Both victims, whose identities have not been disclosed, had 'significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration', MDHHS said in a news release. The department said no further details on the two cases would be released. MDHHS reported 11,234 confirmed cyclosporiasis cases as of 3 August, up from 10,773 just three days earlier, with 193 people hospitalised since late July. Michigan typically logs around 50 cases of the illness in an entire year, making this outbreak more than 200 times the state's normal annual total.
The FDA said it was aware of the fatalities and was coordinating with Michigan officials. A spokesperson said that, based on information supplied by Michigan officials, both individuals 'had illness onset dates prior to the date of Taylor Farms de Mexico's voluntary recall on 17 July 2026'. Cyclosporiasis is caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, which spreads through food or water contaminated with human faeces and typically triggers severe, watery diarrhoea.
Dr William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said the parasite's danger lies chiefly in fluid loss. He noted that dehydration from persistent diarrhoea and vomiting can become life-threatening, particularly in people who already have compromised health, though the illness is usually treated successfully with the antibiotic Bactrim.
Lettuce Recall and Traceback Investigation
MDHHS and the FDA have identified shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico as the probable source of the outbreak, though the link has not been definitively confirmed. Taylor Farms issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on 17 July 2026, after a traceback investigation pointed to the supplier.

Despite that reversal, the FDA has continued to treat the lettuce supply chain as the most likely source, and MDHHS has said lettuce or salad greens remain a probable, though not definitively confirmed, vector for the wider outbreak.
Nationally, the CDC has recorded more than 4,100 laboratory-confirmed cases since 1 May, with a further 7,400 likely cases under investigation across dozens of states. sources.text:
Two people in Michigan have died from cyclosporiasis, state health officials announced on Aug. 3. They are the first reported deaths from a record Cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands of people across the U.S.
“The reported deaths are a sobering reminder that cyclosporiasis is usually not life-threatening, but it can become very serious in vulnerable individuals,” says Rodney E. Rohde, chair of the Medical Laboratory Science Program at Texas State University.
The two people who died had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” according to an update on the Michigan health department’s website. The health department said it wouldn’t provide additional information on the two cases.
The U.S. is experiencing the largest Cyclospora outbreak in its recorded history, with more than 18,000 cases confirmed or suspected across 45 states since May 1, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Michigan, which has been particularly hard-hit by the pathogen, is at the center of a multi-state spate of cases linked to shredded iceberg lettuce. More than 11,200 cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported in the state since June 22, and more than 190 people have been hospitalized, according to Michigan officials.
Cyclospora is a parasite that spreads through human feces, typically via contaminated food and water. It can cause frequent, watery, and explosive diarrhea that can last days or weeks. More than 400 people have been hospitalized from cyclosporiasis across the country since the outbreak began, according to the CDC. Deaths from the parasite are uncommon in the U.S., food-safety experts say.
“While most people recover from cyclosporiasis, individuals with underlying medical conditions or those in higher-risk groups may be more susceptible to serious complications, especially if prolonged diarrhea results in dehydration,” says Wade Syers, a food-safety specialist at Michigan State University Extension. “Anyone experiencing persistent diarrhea, signs of dehydration, or worsening symptoms should seek medical attention, particularly if they are in a higher-risk group.”
People who are elderly or have weakened immune systems, including people who are undergoing chemotherapy or who have advanced HIV, are at greater risk of cyclosporiasis complications, says Rohde. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics, along with aggressive fluid replacement when needed, can significantly reduce the risks of complications, he says.
To reduce potential exposure to Cyclospora, food-safety experts recommend buying intact heads of lettuce and whole fruits and vegetables over bagged, boxed, or pre-cut produce. They also advise people to wash produce thoroughly under running water and follow other food-safety best practices, such as keeping raw meat and vegetables separate when preparing and cooking food. Cooking food to an internal temperature of at least 158°F can kill Cyclospora.
Rohde says people should follow food-safety guidance to keep themselves safe from foodborne illnesses, but for most healthy people, “these deaths should increase awareness, not panic,” he says.

Foods previously linked to Cyclospora outbreaks include:

“The way this spreads is from a person having diarrhea and some of that material getting into either food prep or food service,” said Goldberg.
Cyclospora infections are seasonal, with cases rising in spring and summer. The cyclosporiasis season runs from May 1 to Aug. 31.
FDA investigations of foodborne illness outbreaks have recorded 21 cases related to Cyclospora outbreaks since 2013. The most common food items are fresh herbs and leafy vegetables found in salad mixes.
Which food has been linked to past Cyclospora outbreaks?
Goldberg said the best way to prevent cyclospora is to do more than just rinse food under running water. He said to manually clean the surface of the food, but not to use bleach or surface-cleaning agents.
“If you’re going to a farmer’s market or other area and you purchase food, that food has to have a prep process other than just soaking in water. It needs to be washed with a forceful water flow and manually cleaned,” said Goldberg.
What are symptoms of cyclosporiasis?
“There are multiple organisms that can cause diarrhea,” said Goldberg. “What makes cyclospora different is that it causes explosive diarrhea.”
The CDC website lists some symptoms of cyclosporiasis to watch for:
- Watery diarrhea (most common)
- Loss of appetite
- Weight loss
- Cramping
- Bloating
- Increased gas
- Nausea
- Fatigue
Less common symptoms may include:
- Vomiting
- Body aches
- Headache
- Low-grade fever
- Other flu-like symptoms
For most people, cyclosporiasis lasts days, but some with persistent or severe infections may need antibiotics to clear it. Goldberg said people should seek medical care if they have a fever, persistent nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, or are unable to keep up with fluids.
How to prevent cyclospora?
The CDC has these prevention tips people can follow to help prevent foodborne illness related to fresh produce:
Wash
- Wash hands with soap and water before and after handling or preparing raw fruits and vegetables.
Prepare
- Wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly under running water before eating, cutting, or cooking.
- Fruits and vegetables that are labeled "prewashed" do not need to be washed again at home.
- Scrub firm fruits and vegetables, such as melons and cucumbers, with a clean produce brush.
- Cut away any damaged or bruised areas on fruits and vegetables before preparing and eating.
Store
- Refrigerate cut, peeled or cooked fruits and vegetables as soon as possible, within two hours.
There is currently no evidence of a single multistate Cyclospora outbreak linking all cases.
But in recent years, the CDC says the number of reported U.S. cases has been increasing as the parasite has been found on domestically grown produce.
“We’re seeing now this year an acceleration of food-related illness in the United States. We don’t have a single explanation for it. It’s not clear if it is coming from farms or if there are other sources involved,” Goldberg said.

DETROIT — Two people have died from the massive cyclosporiasis outbreak in Michigan, state health officials reported Monday, though they provided few details about the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
The deaths appear to be the first reported by a state health department in the United States amid this summer's cyclosporiasis outbreak, which started in late June and has hit multiple states hard. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded no deaths through July 27.
Officials with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said the individuals who died had "significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration." But they said no other details, including the location of the deaths, would be released.
"No additional information will be provided on these two cases," the department said.
The number of cyclosporiasis cases in Michigan, meanwhile, continues to rise. State health officials on Monday reported that there have been 11,234 cases of the parasitic illness in Michigan since June 22. That's an 8% increase over last Thursday's case total of 10,386. It's the largest outbreak of cyclosporiasis to ever hit Michigan.
State health officials said cyclosporiasis, which usually causes frequent, watery explosive diarrhea, is generally not a life-threatening illness.
"Death resulting from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States," the department said.
The outbreak has been linked to contaminated lettuce, and dozens of counties in Michigan have been impacted. As of last Thursday, 193 people had reportedly been hospitalized, according to the state health department. The CDC has recorded 423 hospitalizations nationwide through July 27.
But after daily cases peaked July 13 with 726 in one day, the number of cases of cyclosporiasis reported each day to the state health department has declined.
The CDC, the Food and Drug Administration and state public health officials have been investigating a link between the outbreak and iceberg lettuce from central Mexico. The outbreak has hit nine states, including Indiana, Kentucky, Ohio, West Virginia, Kansas, Illinois, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania.
The CDC said it's also investigating other outbreaks and illnesses of cyclosporiasis nationally that are unrelated to that outbreak.
Cases spread to Canada
Meanwhile, the Windsor-Essex County Health Unit in Canada, which covers the city of Windsor, Essex County and Pelee Island, said on Friday that it had identified 24 cases of cyclosporiasis in 2026. The region averages around three cases in a typical year. The health unit said that local public health investigations have identified travel to Michigan as a common exposure among many recent cases.
"The Windsor-Essex County Health Unit (WECHU) is advising residents to take precautions when travelling to Michigan following a significant increase in cases of cyclosporiasis reported locally and throughout the State of Michigan," the agency said in a news release.
What to do about lettuce during outbreak
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services recommends buying whole heads of lettuce or salad greens instead of bagged lettuce, removing the outer leaves, trimming any damaged areas and washing the produce thoroughly before eating it.
The state health department said in an FAQ document that while the investigation is ongoing, current results point to lettuce or salad greens as a potential source for this outbreak, "although other food items cannot be completely ruled out." Past Cyclospora outbreaks have been linked to raspberries, basil, cilantro, snow peas and mesclun lettuce.
"Continue to follow general food safety practices for all fresh produce: Wash it, peel it if you can, cook it," the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said. "Do not assume that any specific item is 'cleared' unless public health authorities explicitly say so."
