The CDC says the illness, called cyclosporiasis, is rarely deadly.
The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water.
Dr. Joel Kammeyer, the division chief of infectious diseases at Wayne State University and the Detroit Medical Center, called the deaths a “tragedy” but noted that despite thousands of cyclosporiasis cases, only two people have died.
“For someone who comes into an urgent care and cyclosporiasis is their only issue, it’s relatively easy to treat,” Kammeyer said. But for people who are struggling with other illnesses, he said, “it stands to reason that there are some patients that might not be able to withstand the dehydration that can come with severe cyclosporiasis.”
Cyclosporiasis is less common than other foodborne illnesses, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source and, for years, few U.S. cyclospora outbreaks were reported. But the number started rising about a decade ago, with a particularly notable spike in 2018 and 2019.
Previously, 2019 saw the most reported U.S. cyclosporiasis cases, with about 4,700.

According to the CDC, the 2026 cyclospora season has seen an unusually large increase in illnesses nationwide. The deaths come as Michigan's outbreak continues to grow. As of August 3, MDHHS reported 11,234 cases statewide and 193 hospitalizations. The true number of infections may be even higher because many people recover without seeking medical care or are never tested for the parasite.

Public health officials have not advised consumers to avoid all fresh produce, but they are urging people to pay close attention to outbreak notices and recalls. In the current U.S. outbreaks, investigators have linked illnesses to products containing iceberg lettuce, prompting several recalls from Taylor Farms. Consumers should check for ongoing FDA and CDC updates and avoid any recalled products or foods identified as part of outbreak investigations.
Newsweek reached out to Taylor Farms by email for comment.
Cyclospora is spread when food or water becomes contaminated with the microscopic parasite, often before it reaches consumers. While washing fruits and vegetables is always recommended, experts note that Cyclospora can be particularly difficult to remove completely through rinsing alone. If a specific product is implicated in an outbreak, the safest approach is to avoid eating it until health officials determine the contamination risk has passed.
For people who want to be especially cautious about Cyclospora exposure during an outbreak, fruits and vegetables with thick, removable outer peels are generally considered a lower-risk option because any contamination is more likely to remain on the surface that is discarded before eating. Examples include bananas, oranges, avocados, melons, and mangoes.
Cooking is the most reliable way to kill or inactivate the parasite, making thoroughly cooked fruits and vegetables a safer choice than raw produce during an outbreak.
What Is Causing the Cyclospora Outbreak?
Cyclospora infections are caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis. People become sick after consuming food or water contaminated with the parasite, which is most commonly associated with fresh produce. Unlike many foodborne bacteria, Cyclospora typically requires days to weeks in the environment before it becomes infectious, meaning the parasite is generally not spread directly from one sick person to another.
The source of contamination in each outbreak can vary and is often difficult to identify. Investigators frequently trace cases to fresh fruits, vegetables, herbs, or leafy greens that may have been exposed to contaminated water or unsanitary conditions during growing, harvesting, or processing. Cyclospora infection, known as cyclosporiasis, most commonly causes prolonged, watery diarrhea that can be explosive. Other symptoms can include loss of appetite, stomach cramps, bloating, nausea, fatigue, weight loss, and sometimes a low-grade fever. Symptoms often begin about a week after a person consumes contaminated food, though the timing can vary from person to person.
Without treatment, symptoms can last for days or even weeks and may come and go over time. The standard treatment is the antibiotic combination trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), according to the CDC. Most people recover fully with appropriate treatment, but anyone experiencing severe diarrhea, dehydration, persistent symptoms, or signs of illness after eating recalled products should contact a healthcare provider. Two people in Michigan have died amid cyclosporiasis outbreak, perhaps first in US
Two people with cyclosporiasis have died amid Michigan's largest outbreak of the parasitic illness, state health officials reported Monday, though they provided few details about the circumstances surrounding the deaths, including the counties in which they occurred or the victims' ages.
Officials with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said Monday the individuals who died had "significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration." But they said no other details, including the location of the deaths, would be released.
"No additional information will be provided on these two cases," the department said.
The deaths appear to be the first reported by a state health department in the United States amid this summer's cyclosporiasis outbreak, which started in late June and has hit multiple states hard. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded no deaths through July 27.
State health officials said cyclosporiasis, which usually causes frequent, watery explosive diarrhea, is generally not a life-threatening illness.
"Death resulting from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States," the Michigan department said.
Dr. Rebecca Schein, an assistant professor in the Department of Pediatrics and Human Development at Michigan State University College of Human Medicine, was more emphatic, saying death from the Cyclospora illness is "extremely rare."
The number of cyclosporiasis cases in Michigan, meanwhile, continues to rise, though they appear to be leveling off. State health officials on Monday reported that there have been 11,234 cases of the parasitic illness in Michigan since June 22, an 8% increase over last Thursday's case total of 10,386. It's the largest outbreak of cyclosporiasis to hit Michigan, which typically has about 50 cases each year.
Michigan is seeing deaths now related to the parasitic illness given the high number of cases it's had, said Dr. Teena Chopra, professor of internal medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Wayne State University School of Medicine in Detroit.
Typically, cyclosporiasis is a treatable illness, but she said people, especially older adults, immunocompromised individuals and those with multiple comorbid illnesses, should go to their doctor if they have diarrhea.
“I would urge people to seek help early on because there is an antibiotic that we can give for it,” Chopra said, referring to the antibiotic Bactrim.
The outbreak has been linked to contaminated lettuce, and 71 counties in Michigan have been impacted. As of last Thursday, 193 people had reportedly been hospitalized, according to the state health department. The CDC has recorded 423 hospitalizations nationwide through July 27.
But after daily cases peaked July 13 with 726 in one day, the number of cases of cyclosporiasis reported each day to the state health department has declined.
In Michigan, the largest case totals are in Wayne County with 1,625 cases, Oakland County with 1,043 cases, Washtenaw County with 875 cases, and Ingham County with 810 cases.
The CDC, the Food and Drug Administration and state public health officials have been investigating a link between the outbreak and iceberg lettuce grown by Taylor Farms in central Mexico. The outbreak has hit nine states, including Indiana, Kentucky, Ohio, West Virginia, Kansas, Illinois, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania.
In late July, Taylor Farms temporarily shut down its Central Mexico processing facility linked to the outbreak. It produces 5-pound bags of shredded iceberg lettuce sold to Taco Bell, Sysco and other large food distributors that Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled on July 17.
Cases spread to Canada
Meanwhile, the Windsor-Essex County Health Unit in Canada, which covers the city of Windsor, Essex County and Pelee Island, said Friday that it had identified 24 cases of cyclosporiasis in 2026. The region averages around three cases in a typical year. The health unit said that local public health investigations have identified travel to Michigan as a common exposure among many recent cases.
"The Windsor-Essex County Health Unit (WECHU) is advising residents to take precautions when travelling to Michigan following a significant increase in cases of cyclosporiasis reported locally and throughout the State of Michigan," the agency said in a news release.
How cyclosporiasis affects the body
Wayne State's Chopra said Cyclospora, the parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, invades people’s intestinal cells. She said it can cause severe dehydration. People lose electrolytes when they are dehydrated.
“Now, if we are healthy, we can compensate,” she said. “Our bodies can compensate.”
But people who are older than 65 don’t “have the same immune system to fight the infection,” and their bodies are more vulnerable to dehydration, Chopra said.
Dehydration affects other organs in the body, Chopra said. Cyclosporiasis can be a contributing cause to a person’s death, she said. Chopra said for a patient with heart disease, for example, cyclosporiasis can worsen their heart disease, which can lead to complications.
MSU's Stein said Cyclospora causes watery diarrhea that can last for days to weeks. She noted that diarrhea, especially if it lasts a long time, can cause dehydration.
"When you are dehydrated, that can damage your kidneys," she said in a statement. "For most people this is not a big problem, but if you have health issues and especially kidney problems, complications can occur."
What to do about lettuce during outbreak
To avoid more cases, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services recommends buying whole heads of lettuce or salad greens instead of bagged lettuce, removing the outer leaves, trimming any damaged areas and washing the produce thoroughly before eating it.
The state health department said in an FAQ document that while the investigation is ongoing, current results point to lettuce or salad greens as a potential source for this outbreak, "although other food items cannot be completely ruled out." Past Cyclospora outbreaks have been linked to raspberries, basil, cilantro, snow peas and mesclun lettuce.
"Continue to follow general food safety practices for all fresh produce: Wash it, peel it if you can, cook it," the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said. "Do not assume that any specific item is 'cleared' unless public health authorities explicitly say so."

Two deaths in Michigan were linked to the cyclosporiasis outbreak, as more than 11,000 cases were reported across the state.
On Aug. 3, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) reported 11,234 cyclosporiasis cases since June 22, up from 10,773 on July 31. Of those reported cases, 193 were hospitalized as of July 30.

According to state health officials and medical health records, two people who had significant underlying health conditions have died and may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration. No further information was released.

The CDC said cases have been identified in 34 states and expects illnesses to continue increasing through the end of August, when the typical Cyclospora season ends.
“Anyone experiencing gastrointestinal illness, such as sudden and ongoing diarrhea, should contact their health care provider and their local health department,” MDHHS said in a statement.
While MDHHS and local health officials are still working to identify the direct source of the growing outbreak, they said lettuce or salad greens could be a possible source.
What is cyclosporiasis?
Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by a parasite and infects the small intestine.
Healthcare providers can diagnose the illness by testing a stool sample.
If infected with cyclosporiasis, people may experience watery diarrhea with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements. People can also experience symptoms like fatigue, nausea, stomach cramps and loss of appetite.
The illness can last from a few days to over a month if the illness is not treated. Symptoms could relapse.
The timeframe from becoming infected to becoming sick usually takes about one week but can range from two days to two weeks or more.
In the US, outbreaks of cyclosporiasis have been linked to various types of fresh produce. People can get infected with Cyclospora more than once.
Anyone who experiences symptoms of cyclosporiasis should see their healthcare provider.
Related --> 6 things Michiganders are getting wrong about the cyclosporiasis outbreak
Precautions with lettuce, salad greens
MDHHS said, based on early information in the outbreak investigation and the historical link to Cyclospora and pre-packaged salad greens, they recommend people practice the following safety measures with lettuce:
- Purchase whole heads: Buy whole heads of lettuce rather than pre-washed, bagged lettuce or pre-mixed salad kits.
- Discard outer layers: Before preparation, throw away the outer two to three layers of leaves.
- Wash inner leaves: Thoroughly wash the remaining inner leaves under clean running water.
- Prioritize cooking: For any greens that can be cooked, cooking to a temperature of at least 158 F (70 C) is the safest option, as the parasite is resistant to routine chemical disinfection and washing alone cannot guarantee its removal.
Produce linked to previous outbreaks
Health officials said the following foods have been previously linked to Cyclospora outbreaks in the United States and Canada:
- Bagged salad mixes and kits (pre-cut lettuce blends with romaine, iceberg, red cabbage, carrots)
- Fresh cilantro (coriander leaves)
- Fresh basil
- Raspberries
- Snow peas
- Green onions (scallions)
Produce recommendations
MDHHS provided a list of recommendations on preparing, processing or serving raw produce, including restaurants and other commercial kitchens.
Health officials said to take the following steps to reduce risk of exposure:
- Cilantro, basil: Wash thoroughly under running water, separating the leaves. Safest when cooked.
- Green onions: Trim the root end and remove the outer layer, wash thoroughly under running water. Safest when cooked.
- Raspberries: Their bumpy surface makes them especially hard to clean; the parasite can hide in the tiny crevices. Safest when cooked (pies, jams etc.). Consider frozen raspberries as an alternative (freezing may reduce but does not guarantee elimination of the parasite).
- Snow peas: Wash under running water and rub the surface. Safest when cooked.
MDHHS said the recommendations are essential for people who have a higher risk of dehydration or weakened immune systems, such as patients on chemotherapy, organ transplant recipients, infants and young children and elderly people.
General rules, routine food practices
Health officials said general rules of thumb to reduce the risk of getting the illness are to cook food -- when you can -- to 158 degrees or higher to kill cyclospora, and wash all fresh produce under clean running water, even if you plan to peel it.
Food safety reminders
Here are some reminders on food safety practices, according to the MDHHS:
- Wash hands with soap and water before and after handling or preparing food.
- Scrub firm fruits and vegetables, such as melons and cucumbers, with a clean produce brush.
- Cut away any damaged or bruised areas on fruits and vegetables before preparing and eating.
- Wash and sanitize utensils and surfaces before and after handling food. Wash and sanitize display cases and refrigerators where fresh produce is stored.
- Wash and sanitize cutting boards, surfaces and utensils used to prepare, serve or store fresh produce.
- Refrigerate cut, peeled or cooked fruits and vegetables as soon as possible.

Michigan has reported up to 11,234 cases of cyclosporiasis in the current outbreak, though Malani says the true number is likely higher, because many people whose symptoms are milder don't seek testing or treatment.
As of July 30, there have been 193 reported hospitalizations in Michigan. Malani says many of the people he and his colleagues have seen are elderly and have underlying conditions, including cardiac and lung disease, cancer and liver disease.
"I will say that the large, overwhelming majority of people that have cyclospora have done well" and recovered, Malani says.
He says he and his colleagues have seen a marked slowdown in the number of people testing positive for cyclosporiasis compared to three weeks ago, when they were seeing "well over 100 people" a day on some days.
Nationally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 6,707 confirmed cases as of July. The number is lower than what states collectively are reporting because of the time it takes for local health authorities to pass information to the federal level and for federal officials to investigate and confirm.
The CDC and the Food and Drug Administration are investigating cases in 45 states. It's the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record in the U.S.
Health officials recommend people follow standard food safety handling protocols to protect themselves from the parasite. Cooking fruits and vegetables to 158 degrees F will also kill the parasite.

995 Cyclospora Cases Reported in Illinois as Michigan Sees First 2 US Deaths Related to Outbreak
Two people have died in the cyclospora outbreak in Michigan, state health officials announced Monday, the first deaths confirmed in the U.S. related to the microscopic parasite.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said both people had underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by the intestinal illness and dehydration. The department said it would not provide additional information about the deaths.
In Illinois, there have been no deaths related to the cyclospora outbreak, the Illinois Department of Public Health reported Tuesday. The state has seen 995 confirmed and probable cases of cyclosporiasis as of Tuesday. IDPH updates cyclosporiasis case numbers every Tuesday.
Illinois reported 58 hospitalizations as a result of the illness, as of Tuesday.
In Chicago, 209 confirmed and probable cases of cyclosporiasis were reported as of Monday, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health. Pending ongoing investigation, at least 15 cases have been linked to the multi-state lettuce outbreak, and 103 cases were likely acquired locally, according to a CDPH spokesperson.
Among the local cases, CDPH has not yet found a specific source, a spokesperson said.
In late July, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention added Illinois as part of a multi-state outbreak of cyclosporiasis linked to iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico and recalled by Taylor Farms de Mexico. The other states included in the specific outbreak were Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
“While no single source has been identified for all cases, a number of people reporting illness in Illinois said they had consumed shredded lettuce while dining out,” according to an IDPH statement. “Products that are suspected of being part of the outbreak are now being removed from restaurants, retail stores, and other food service locations, and IDPH is hopeful that those actions and increased public awareness will lead to fewer cases in the days ahead.”
Cyclosporiasis is a gastrointestinal disease caused by the parasite cyclospora, which can cause frequent and watery diarrhea. The disease is spread by consuming contaminated food or water.
Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.
Cyclosporiasis is less common than other foodborne illnesses, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source and, for years, few U.S. cyclospora outbreaks were reported. But the number started rising about a decade ago, with a particularly notable spike in 2018 and 2019.
Previously, 2019 saw the most reported U.S. cyclosporiasis cases, with about 4,700.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it is aware of more than 18,000 confirmed or suspected cases in the current surge. But CDC numbers can lag state reports, which suggest the number is more than 20,000 nationwide.
Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in nine states as a source of the widespread outbreak. As of late July, the number of cases linked to the lettuce was 1,947, including at least 98 people who had to be hospitalized, according to the CDC.
The agency has said other “brands, restaurants, retailers, or distribution channels” could be tied to the outbreak as the investigation continues.
Public health officials recommend the following to protect yourself:
- Follow guidance on product recalls, including voluntary recalls, and avoid consuming products linked to outbreaks
- Wash your hands with soap and water before and after handling or preparing food
- Wash all fresh produce under running water before eating, cutting or cooking
- Scrub firm fruits and vegetables with a produce brush
- Wash and sanitize utensils and surfaces before and after handling food
- Remove any damaged or bruised areas before preparing and eating
- Refrigerate cut, peeled or cooked fruits and vegetables within 2 hours
- Cook produce to 158 degrees Fahrenheit to kill cyclospora
Cyclosporiasis can be treated with an antibiotic, but in most healthy people, it can go away on its own and might not require treatment, according to CDPH medical director Dr. Janna Kerins. Individuals who are very young, older adults, those with a weakened immune system or who have a chronic underlying disease are at higher risk for severe illness.

The cyclosporiasis outbreak just turned deadly.
Two people died in Michigan after contracting cyclosporiasis, the state’s health department announced Monday. They’re the first confirmed deaths in the country that have been tied to the public health crisis spurred by a single-celled parasite found on iceberg lettuce.
Both people had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement, noting that no additional information about the specific cases will be shared.
“Cyclosporiasis is generally not a life-threatening illness,” the statement continued. “Death resulting from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States.”
So far, the state health agency has tallied 11,234 cases and 193 confirmed hospitalizations associated with the illness.
Those numbers would indicate that federal health agencies are far behind in their own analysis of the parasite’s spread—or, at the very least, are failing to inform the American people as to the true nature of the nationwide threat. As of Monday, the CDC’s “fast facts” page on cyclosporiasis recorded “at least 1,947” cases and 98 hospitalizations across nine states.
In a July 28 memo, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said that it had received reports of at least 6,707 laboratory-confirmed domestic cases of cyclosporiasis, though an additional 11,500 cases had not yet been confirmed.
An analysis by The New Republic of state health agency data found at least 18,517 cases across the nine states listed by the CDC. The survey compiled reported figures from Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia. However, several of those states had not updated their own public-facing data within days or even weeks, suggesting that the current case tally could be much higher.
Health officials said that anyone experiencing symptoms should reach out to a health care provider right away. Symptoms of cyclosporiasis can include sudden, prolonged diarrhea; bloating, severe stomach cramps, loss of appetite, extreme lethargy, and even a low-grade fever, though many people infected by the parasite show no symptoms at all, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Those most at risk of serious illness from the parasite are the elderly, infants, and people with compromised immune systems.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Thursday that public health investigators were having a difficult time tracking the disease as it can take people one to two weeks to exhibit symptoms after the consumption of infected food.

Two people are dead as Michigan's cyclosporiasis cases top 11K in nine state outbreak
Two people are dead as the state's largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak continues.
On Monday, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) announced that two Michiganders who contracted cyclosporiasis, a parasitic infection caused by the parasite Cyclospora, are dead, and the total number of reported cases is up to 11, 234 after surpassing 10,000 on Wednesday with 193 hospitalizations.
Both people who died had "significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration," according to health officials. No additional details are being released by MDHHS about the people who died.
One of the biggest risks surrounding cyclosporiasis is dehydration, as the infection causes frequent watery, "explosive" diarrhea, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Though the infection is not usually deadly, people with certain preexisting conditions or antibiotic allergies can struggle to recover.
Michigan is one of nine states experiencing a major outbreak of cyclosporiasis linked to shredded lettuce supplied to Taco Bell by Taylor Farms' central Mexico facility.
Despite some confusion from a false-positive test result of Taylor Farms lettuce, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said the produce supplier and Taco Bell are both still at the center of their investigation.
FDA officials said there is "overwhelming" data from their traceback investigation that supports lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms to Taco Bell as the source of the outbreak, though they have not yet announced any positive product test results for Cyclospora.

No Taylor Farms branded salads or kits are associated with the recall.
Taco Bell stopped serving and using ingredients in certain states that could be implicated in the outbreak as a precaution, almost a week before the FDA linked their shredded lettuce to the outbreak. After the FDA implicated them in the outbreak, company officials said they removed all Taylor Farms lettuce from their restaurants in the impacted states and, out of caution, nationwide.
States typically report some amount of cyclosporiasis every infection season. Michigan sees about 50 a year, with the season lasting May 1 to Aug. 31.
This season, however, is shaping up to be the largest number of cases in U.S. history. The CDC said they are investigating multiple clusters of Cyclospora cases, but as of Monday, have only confirmed the one outbreak that includes nine states and is linked to Taylor Farms and Taco Bell.

Philadelphia's Department of Public Health has logged 13 confirmed cyclospora cases as of July 29, placing the city among dozens of jurisdictions tracking the parasite's spread across the country. Nationwide, more than 4,100 lab-confirmed infections have been reported, though health officials note the true number is likely higher since many people recover without seeking medical attention.
A department spokesperson told WHYY the 13 Philadelphia cases span more than just the current outbreak. Some were confirmed before the outbreak began, and others involve residents who most likely contracted the illness while traveling outside the city or abroad.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has linked most confirmed U.S. cases to iceberg lettuce products from Taylor Farms, sold through Taco Bell locations. The source remains largely contained to that supply chain for now.

Local produce suppliers say they have not received any purchase restrictions. Michael Anastasio, who owns a South Philadelphia wholesale operation supplying more than 60 area restaurants, told WHYY his business would be notified by its distribution center and the U.S. Department of Agriculture if any contaminated product entered his supply. Shoppers, however, are less at ease. A Mount Airy resident interviewed by WHYY described the situation as frightening, noting how often lettuce appears in everyday meals and how much remains unknown about the parasite.

Some Philadelphia-area grocers are highlighting their local supply chains as a source of confidence for customers. Weavers Way Co-op, which operates locations in Ambler and the Philadelphia area, sources much of its produce from farms in Lancaster, New Jersey, and even from W.B. Saul Agricultural High School in Roxborough. The co-op also partners with Mort Brooks Memorial Farm at Awbury Arboretum and its own farm market.
Karl Smith, the Ambler location's manager, told WHYY that sourcing locally means any problem in the supply chain would surface quickly. Other Philadelphia businesses focused on regional produce include Riverwards Produce and Philly Foodworks.
What Shoppers Should Know
The CDC advises that cyclospora is not spread person to person. Infections typically cause watery diarrhea, fatigue, and stomach cramps, and the illness can last weeks if untreated. Because symptoms may not appear for up to two weeks after exposure, cases can be difficult to trace back to a specific meal or location.

Written by MIKE HOUSEHOLDER and SUDHIN THANAWALA Associated Press
Two people have died in the cyclospora outbreak in Michigan, state health officials announced Monday, the first deaths confirmed in the U.S. related to the microscopic parasite.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said both people had underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by the intestinal illness and dehydration. The department said it would not provide additional information about the deaths.
Cyclospora is a microscopic, spherical parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Outbreaks tend to occur most often in the late spring and summer.
The CDC says the illness, called cyclosporiasis, is rarely deadly.
The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water.
Dr. Joel Kammeyer, the division chief of infectious diseases at Wayne State University and the Detroit Medical Center, called the deaths a “tragedy” but noted that despite thousands of cyclosporiasis cases, only two people have died.
“For someone who comes into an urgent care and cyclosporiasis is their only issue, it’s relatively easy to treat,” Kammeyer said. But for people who are struggling with other illnesses, he said, “it stands to reason that there are some patients that might not be able to withstand the dehydration that can come with severe cyclosporiasis.”
Cyclosporiasis is less common than other foodborne illnesses, including salmonella and E. coli. Many cases are never linked to a specific food or other source and, for years, few U.S. cyclospora outbreaks were reported. But the number started rising about a decade ago, with a particularly notable spike in 2018 and 2019.
Previously, 2019 saw the most reported U.S. cyclosporiasis cases, with about 4,700.
The CDC said it is aware of more than 18,000 confirmed or suspected cases in the current surge. But CDC numbers can lag state reports, which suggest the number is more than 20,000 nationwide.
Federal health officials have identified lettuce from Mexico served at Taco Bell locations in nine states as a source of the widespread outbreak. As of late July, the number of cases linked to the lettuce was 1,947, including at least 98 people who had to be hospitalized, according to the CDC.
